title: The five in authority
hookLine: decisions are made through five chosen Sikhs

lines: FIVE WALK AHEAD OF THE PROCESSION.
FIVE AT AMRIT, FIVE AT TANKHAH.
cards: Drums first, then flags. A street has been cleared for a nagar kirtan, a Sikh procession: families in their best clothes, a float carrying the Guru Granth Sahib under a canopy.
And walking out front, ahead of everything, five Sikhs dressed alike, swords held upright. Those five lead.
Count back through this block and the number keeps turning up: five who give amrit, five who hear a confession and set a tankhah. It isn't decoration.
In the Sikh way of doing things, when something weighty must be decided, it goes to five.

teach.h: AT CHAMKAUR, THE GURU OBEYED THE FIVE.
teach.b: Begin where the number begins: the panj pyare, the five beloved ones at Anandpur.

In the tradition's telling, the Tenth Guru not only initiated them but asked to be initiated by them, and at Chamkaur, as this path told long ago, the five ordered the Guru to leave the fort, and he obeyed.
So from the start, five chosen Sikhs could speak with an authority the Guru himself honored.

teach.h: FIVE GIVE AMRIT, FIVE SET TANKHAH.
teach.b: The Sikh Rehat Maryada carries that into ordinary life: when amrit is given, five give it; when a breach is confessed, five decide the tankhah. Three things about how it works.

teach.h: CHOSEN FOR THE TASK, NOT BY RANK.
teach.b: First, the five are chosen for the task, from among Sikhs who keep the code. The authority belongs to the role, not the person's rank; a shopkeeper can stand beside a scholar.
Second, five is enough that no single will can rule the room, and few enough to actually sit together and decide. One person can be swayed by a grudge, a crowd by a mood. Five have to talk.

teach.h: THE SAME SHAPE AT THE AKAL TAKHT.
teach.b: At the Akal Takht, the heads of the Takhts and senior granthis can sit together as five, the Panj Singh Sahiban, to decide matters for the whole panth.
A village sangat and the throne of the Timeless use the same shape. Behind it is the conviction this block keeps returning to: the Guru is present where the Khalsa gathers.

how: Sikhs bring weighty decisions to five chosen Sikhs, the panj pyare, who give amrit, set tankhah and lead processions; at the Akal Takht, the Panj Singh Sahiban decide matters for the panth.

games.q: what does “the five in authority” mean?
o: five elders who inherit their seats from their fathers
five chosen Sikhs who decide weighty matters together
five rules of conduct that every Sikh must keep daily

games.q: where the five appear: tap the pairs.
p: the five told the Guru to leave
five walk ahead of the procession
five who decide at the Akal Takht

s: the five are chosen because of their family's rank
they're chosen for the task from Sikhs who keep the code. a shopkeeper can stand beside a scholar.
in the tradition's telling, the Guru obeyed the five at Chamkaur
the five ordered him to leave the fort, and he did.
the five appear only at the amrit ceremony
five give amrit, set tankhah, lead processions and decide at the Akal Takht.

games.q: you're the Tenth Guru at Chamkaur. five of your Sikhs tell you to leave the fort. what do you do?
o: ask the whole army to vote.
games.why: in the tradition's telling, the Guru obeyed. the five he had knelt to at Anandpur spoke with authority he honored.

practice: Bring to mind one small decision you've been carrying alone, and picture four people you trust sitting around it with you, not to vote it away from you but to talk.
Hear each of them ask you one question, and notice which question you'd rather not answer; stay with that one.

wordCard.voice: The five in authority. In Sikh practice, weighty decisions go to five chosen Sikhs, from the amrit ceremony to the Akal Takht. Today's word.
